History and Physical (H&P – Detailed)

Consult Summary:
62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension presents via telemedicine with a 5-day history of dry cough and continuous greenish rhinorrhoea, subjective fever/chills, and myalgias; assessment most consistent with an acute viral upper respiratory tract infection with safety-netting advice provided.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Dry cough and streaming nasal discharge for ~5 days.  
• Onset/progression: Began abruptly 5 days ago; cough persists every 20–30 min; nasal discharge ongoing.  
• Character: Cough dry, non-productive; nasal discharge described as “pretty green.”  
• Associated symptoms: Subjective fever (feels hot to touch) with intermittent chills, myalgias, transient diarrhoea at onset (resolved).  
• Pertinent negatives: No sputum production, haemoptysis, chest pain, dyspnoea, pleuritic pain, sore throat, ear pain, headache, visual changes, vomiting, current diarrhoea, rash.  
• Exacerbating/relieving: Lemsip 2–3 sachets/day gives transient throat relief; no other OTC treatments.  
• Functional intake: Eating, drinking, and urination normal.

Past Medical History:
• Type 2 diabetes mellitus – last blood tests 3 weeks ago reportedly normal; no home glucose monitoring.  
• Hypertension – duration not stated; last BP check “a while ago,” stability unknown.  
• No chronic pulmonary disease.

Medications:
• Metformin – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Lisinopril – patient states “200” (likely miss-stated; exact dose/route/frequency not documented).  
• PRN Lemsip cold remedy (contains paracetamol) – 2–3 sachets/day.  
Allergies: No known drug allergies. Occasional mild hay-fever to environmental allergens.

Social History:
• Lives with partner and dog.  
• Occupation: Office manager.  
• Tobacco: Not documented.  
• Alcohol: “Odd sherry” (minimal).  
• Recreational drugs: Not documented.

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
• Vitals: Not recorded (remote consultation).  
• General/respiratory/ENT exam: Not performed (telemedicine).

Investigations:
• None ordered today.  
• Patient reported routine diabetes labs 3 weeks ago were normal (values not provided).

Assessment & Plan:
Overall Impression:
Acute upper respiratory tract infection, most likely viral (common cold/flu-like illness), in a patient with diabetes and hypertension.

DDx Integration (brief):
1. Acute viral URI/viral bronchitis – abrupt onset, dry cough, rhinorrhoea, myalgias, subjective fever; no focal chest findings (supports).  
2. COVID-19 infection – similar viral presentation; no anosmia/ageusia or dyspnoea reported (partial support).  
3. Acute bacterial sinusitis – green discharge could indicate bacterial component; lacks facial pain/tenderness (partial support).

Issue 1 – Acute viral upper respiratory tract infection
• Advice: Continue symptomatic care (Lemsip ok; avoid other paracetamol-containing products).  
• Obtain thermometer; monitor temperature.  
• Safety-net: Seek medical review if temperature ≥ 37.5–38 °C persists or spikes, cough worsens, develops purulent sputum, haemoptysis, nasal bleeding, chest pain, or shortness of breath.  
• Discussed potential need for antibiotics if bacterial infection suspected at follow-up.

Issue 2 – Type 2 diabetes mellitus
• Ensure regular GP reviews and blood tests; consider obtaining home glucometer for self-monitoring.  
• Monitor for infection-related glycaemic excursions.

Issue 3 – Hypertension
• Encourage blood-pressure review at GP surgery; confirm current lisinopril dose and adherence.

General plan items
• Encourage adequate hydration, rest, and gradual return to normal activity.  
• Consider COVID-19 testing if clinically indicated or per public health advice (not discussed in transcript but may be relevant – conflict noted).  
• Follow-up: Re-contact service or GP if red-flag symptoms occur or no improvement within 1–2 weeks.

Quality checks:
• Missing elements: No vitals, smoking status not clarified, family history not discussed, medication doses incomplete.  
• Conflicts: COVID-19 testing not mentioned by clinician but suggested by DDx (noted).  
• Transcript quality: Clear overall; minor inaudible segments and patient uncertainty about medication dose.
